issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: X509Certificate2Collection.FindByThumbprint for more digest algorithms
comments:
Tagging subscribers to this area: @dotnet/area-system-security, @bartonjs, @vcsjones
See info in [area-owners.md](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/area-owners.md) if you want to be subscribed.
<!-- Policy app identification https://img.shields.io/static/v1?label=PullRequestIssueManagement. -->

Does this not present the same sort of problem down the line, in that the method is tied to one algorithm that will eventually, hopefully long after I retire, end up being broken and banned?

Given that `X509Certificate.GetCertHashString` takes an algorithm name, and we rejected the idea of a [Thumbprint256](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/62425) or other convenience method that baked the algorithm in, would consistency not require a more general FindByThumbprint which takes an algorithm, even if the underlying win32 api only gives us sha1 and sha256 for now?

Actually we can implement it for all hash algorithms, not just SHA-1 and SHA-2-256, so we might as well do that.

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/compare/main...vcsjones:runtime:sha256-find-cert-by-thumbprint-alt

The Win32 SHA256 is apparently new (Windows 10 22H2) so we would need to make it work for older Windowses anyway. Since we are doing that, we can make everything work.
Okay, I like @blowdart's idea more, so I updated the proposal.

If we want this functionality, the proposed shape seems fine. But I'm generally not a fan of X509Certificate2Collection.Find, and so I wonder if we want to invest more in it, or just tell people to use foreach/Linq/etc.

What don't I like?

1. No one understands `validOnly`.  _Clearly_ you only want valid things, right?  Except, it turns out, "valid" includes "this system trusts the certificate chain", which excludes self-signed and "some client cert I have to use when talking to this remote party that I otherwise don't care about".  Also, y'know, expiration and stuff.
2. Find doesn't return the same certificate instances, it returns clones.

```c#
X509Certificate2Collection coll = new() { cert };
X509Certificate2Collection coll2 = coll.Find(FindByThumbprint, cert.Thumbprint, false);
bool same = ReferenceEquals(cert, coll[0]); // true
bool stillSame = ReferenceEquals(cert, coll2[0]); // false
```

Find doesn't _look_ like it allocates finalizable objects, but it does.  And that leads to problems.

```c#
X509Certificate2Collection coll = OpenPFX(bytes, pwd);
coll = coll.Find(FindByThumbprint, thumbprintFromConfig, false);
return coll[0];
```

When does the private key file get erased?  Anyone?  Well... the object that owned cleaning it up got loaded into `coll`. It got cloned by Find.  And the key will be erased:

* .NET 9+: When the original cert gets finalized
* .NET 8-, .NET Framework: When the original cert gets finalized, or the new cert object gets finalized or disposed... whichever of these comes first

Hooray!

---

We have the option of saying "new method, new behavior", and that the new FindByThumbprint should NOT clone the certificates, but copy them into the return collection by reference.  But that would mean `.Find(FindByThumbprint, ...)` and `.FindByThumbprint(...)` were different in that respect, which is probably even more confusing.

End of the day? Probably should Obsolete Find and tell people to use foreach/Linq, especially now that the collection is `IEnumerable<X509Certificate2>`.

> No one understands validOnly.

I am fine nuking that. 

> Find doesn't return the same certificate instances, it returns clones.

In the general case of Find, that is interesting. In the case of FindByThumbprint, though, the typical case is to find exactly one cert. Cloning a single cert seems reasonable to keep the cloning consistency with Find. This API shouldn't result in a whole store being cloned.

That doesn't solve the finalizer / clone by handle issue. So maybe this one just doesn't clone.

> Probably should Obsolete Find 

Maybe. There are some things that Find does that are non-trivial for people to replicate, like all of the gymnastics for serial number. Hex, integer, big endian, little endian... etc. I would think a replacement is due then.

Windows has some feature that adds a CA certificate to a certificate store on demand — IIRC there are certificates embedded in a DLL so that this works even without Internet access.  Does CertFindCertificateInStore trigger that?  If so:

* Replacing Find with System.Linq.Enumerable would break this feature as Windows would no longer know which certificate to add.
* If you call Find with a hash algorithm not supported by CertFindCertificateInStore, then that cannot auto-add the certificate either.

> Does CertFindCertificateInStore trigger that?

It does not. It was a good thought so I double checked. As far as I know, there are two ways to trigger the installation of an on-demand root.

1. Have a copy of it somewhere and have Windows load it, e.g. `CryptQueryObject`. Windows assumes that if you happen to have a full copy of the root certificate lying around and you are interacting with it, it will automatically place it in the root CA store since it is a known root.
2. `CertGetCertificateChain` needs it for path building. In that case it will fetch it.

There may be others, but `CertFindCertificateInStore` is not one of them.

I added overloads that accept the thumbprint as ROS-char (hex) and ROS-byte (actual bytes, since that's what the thumbprint really is).

Private key lifetimes got normalized with the new cert loader, so cloning now is just about GC+finalizer impact.  Since that doesn't have any impact on the API shape (unless someone wants to propose a defaulted boolean that controls the cloning behavior), marking it as ready for review.

> and ROS-byte ...

I don't think we really need support for UTF-8 matches, but if we do we'd have to change the method name between the hex ones and the bytes one.  E.g. FindByThumbprintHex.

review_comments: Since the thumbprint isn't visible here, is it worth asserting that there's at least one non-numeric character?  != on the two strings works, as does IndexOfAnyExcept('0', '1', ..., '9')
I guess so, it would be super funny if the thumbprint worked out to be only numeric digits.
